Romans 9
ROH-muhnz NINE
scripture portion
The ninth chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans; the great Scripture on the sovereignty of God in election.

Biblical Definition

Romans 9 is the fullest treatment in Scripture of the sovereignty of God in election and reprobation. Paul, grieving over unbelieving Israel, defends the faithfulness of God by showing that the promise was never to all Israel after the flesh but to the children of promise. He proves God’s free choice from the patriarchs: before Jacob and Esau were born, having done neither good nor evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, it was said, “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.” The choice rests not on works nor on foreseen faith but on Him that calleth. To the objection that this is unjust, Paul answers that God said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy,” so that it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. He raised up Pharaoh to display His power, and He hardens whom He will. To the further objection, “Why doth he yet find fault?” Paul does not soften but presses: shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? The potter has power over the clay. The dictionary receives Romans 9 as the clearest charter of unconditional election: salvation is of the Lord, His mercy is free and sovereign, and the creature has no claim upon the Creator but owes Him everything.

Webster 1828 Definition

Paul’s fullest treatment of God’s sovereignty in election; salvation rests not on works or foreseen faith but on God who shows mercy, the Potter over the clay.

ROMANS 9, the great chapter on the sovereignty of God in election.

Shows the promise was to the children of promise, not all Israel after the flesh.

Proves free election from Jacob and Esau, chosen before they had done good or evil.

Key Scripture

Rom 9:11 — "(For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)"

Rom 9:15 — "For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion."

Rom 9:16 — "So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy."

Rom 9:21 — "Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?"

Modern Corruption

The chapter’s sovereign election is evaded by reading it as merely national, or as resting on foreseen faith, against Paul’s own argument.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is unconditional election. Paul forecloses every escape: the choice of Jacob over Esau was made before they were born or had done any good or evil, expressly that election might rest on Him that calleth and not on works. To make election depend on foreseen faith or merit is to assert the very thing the chapter denies.

A common evasion reads Romans 9 as concerned only with national destiny—the choice of Israel as a people for an earthly role—and not with the eternal salvation of individuals. But Paul’s grief is over individuals perishing in unbelief, his examples are individuals, and his conclusion is the mercy and hardening of individuals by the sovereign will of God. The dictionary holds the chapter’s plain force, including its hard sayings: God has mercy on whom He will and hardens whom He will, and the clay may not answer back to the Potter.

Hebrew Roots

The chapter’s language of calling, mercy, and the potter sets forth God’s free and sovereign election.

expand to see more

Greek eklogē — election, choice; “the purpose of God according to election.”

Greek eleō — to have mercy; “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.”

Greek sklērunō — to harden; “whom he will he hardeneth.”

The potter and clay image draws on Isaiah and Jeremiah.

“Children of promise” distinguishes the elect from Israel after the flesh.
